♻ ☆ FairMed-XGB: A Bayesian-Optimised Multi-Metric Framework with Explainability for Demographic Equity in Critical Healthcare Data
Mitul Goswami, Romit Chatterjee, Arif Ahmed Sekh
Background:Machine learning models in emergency medicine often exhibit demographic biases, particularly gender disparities, which can compromise fairness, clinical trust, and decision-making reliability. Existing mitigation approaches typically optimise isolated fairness metrics, failing to address the multi-dimensional nature of bias while maintaining predictive performance and interpretability. Methods: We propose FairMed-XGB, a Bayesian-optimised, multi-metric fairness framework integrated into an XGBoost classifier. The model incorporates a composite fairness-aware loss function combining Statistical Parity Difference, Theil Index, and Wasserstein Distance. Bayesian optimisation is used to balance fairness and predictive accuracy. The framework is evaluated on seven cohorts derived from the MIMIC-IV-ED and eICU datasets. SHAP-based explainability is employed to analyse feature contributions and identify bias-related patterns. Results: FairMed-XGB significantly reduces gender-based disparities across all cohorts. Statistical Parity Difference decreases by 40-51% on MIMIC-IV-ED and 10-19% on eICU datasets. Theil Index values reduce by four to five orders of magnitude, approaching near-zero levels, while Wasserstein Distance decreases by 20-72%. These improvements are achieved with minimal impact on predictive performance (AUC-ROC reduction <0.02). SHAP analysis demonstrates reduced dependence on gender-proxy features and improved distributional fairness. Conclusions: FairMed-XGB provides a robust and interpretable framework for mitigating demographic bias in emergency medicine prediction models. By jointly optimising multiple fairness objectives and preserving model performance, it enables equitable and trustworthy AI deployment in high-stakes clinical settings. The integration of explainability further supports transparency and clinical adoption.
♻ ☆ Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting with a Multi-GPU PyTorch Backend
Matthew Cong, Francis Williams, Jonathan Swartz, Mark Harris, Sanja Fidler, Ken Museth
Gaussian splatting methods have become increasingly popular for neural reconstruction of the real world. However, they are often limited in scale and resolution due to compute and memory constraints. We present a multi-GPU Gaussian splatting approach that scales reconstruction to higher resolutions and larger scenes while abstracting away the code complexity typically associated with distributing a model. We demonstrate city-scale reconstructions with street-level detail consisting of over 1 billion Gaussian splats. To accomplish this, we propose a PyTorch backend that distributes parameters and operators across GPUs via CUDA unified memory, with optional NVLink support. Because distribution occurs at the operator level, the model code requires no explicit cross-device communication. More broadly, the backend exposes multiple GPUs as an aggregate asynchronous PyTorch device and supports a broad set of PyTorch operators enabling the distribution of general PyTorch workloads.
comment: 13 pages, 8 tables, 4 figures, and 1 listing. Includes supplementary material
♻ ☆ ASTERISM: Do Multimodal LLMs Actually Look at All the Images?
Chanseul Cho, Dongwoo Kim, Noori Bae, Seungjae Moon, Seongsu Lee, Youngmin Ro
Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.
comment: Code and datasets: https://github.com/chanseul01/ASTERISM
♻ ☆ Improving regional weather forecasts with neural interpolation
James Jackaman, Oliver Sutton
In this paper we design a neural interpolation operator to improve the boundary data for regional weather models, which is a challenging problem as we are required to map multi-scale dynamics between grid resolutions. In particular, we expose a methodology for approaching the problem through the study of a simplified model, with a view to generalise the results in this work to the dynamical core of regional weather models. Our approach will exploit a combination of techniques from image super-resolution with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual networks, in addition to building the flow of atmospheric dynamics into the neural network. We find that building in the flow more than halves the squared error of small networks.
♻ ☆ StochEP: Stochastic Equilibrium Propagation for Spiking Convergent Recurrent Neural Networks
Jiaqi Lin, Yi Jiang, Abhronil Sengupta
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, sparse, biologically inspired computation. Training them with Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) and surrogate gradients achieves strong performance but remains biologically implausible. Equilibrium Propagation (EP) provides a more local and biologically grounded alternative. However, existing EP frameworks for SNNs largely rely on deterministic neurons, which require complex mechanisms to handle spiking discontinuities and do not scale beyond simple benchmarks such as MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Inspired by the stochastic nature of biological spiking mechanism and recent hardware trends, we propose a stochastic EP framework that integrates probabilistic spiking neurons into the EP paradigm. This formulation smoothens the optimization landscape, stabilizes training, and enables efficient and scalable learning in SNNs. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that the proposed stochastic EP dynamics approximate deterministic EP under mean-field theory, thereby inheriting its underlying theoretical guarantees. The proposed framework narrows the performance gap with both BPTT-trained SNNs and EP-trained non-spiking convergent recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) on CIFAR-10, DVS Gesture, and IMDB datasets, while preserving temporal and spatial locality. Our results highlight stochastic EP as a promising approach for neuromorphic and on-chip learning.
♻ ☆ Resolution-free neural surrogates for geometric parameterization and mapping with spatially varying fields
Yanwen Huang, Lok Ming Lui, Gary P. T. Choi
Many imaging problems require computing spatial transformations induced by spatially varying intensity, feature, or density fields. Canonical examples include distortion correction, deformable image registration, atlas-based segmentation, and deformation-driven image analysis. These tasks can be formulated as geometric mapping problems in which the transformation is constrained to preserve local structure, control boundary behavior, or regulate angular distortion. Such formulations typically lead to variational models, diffusion processes, or elliptic partial differential equations. However, repeatedly solving high-resolution systems becomes computationally expensive when the underlying parameter fields vary across instances. In this work, we propose a resolution-free neural surrogate for geometric parameterization and mapping problems. Given a spatially varying parameter field $p:Ω\to\mathbb{R}^m$ and grid nodes $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^N\subsetΩ$, the model predicts mapped locations $\{u(x_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ on structured grids of different sizes without retraining. To avoid dependence on a fixed grid, we use a multi-resolution geometric encoding strategy that conditions the network on coordinate-augmented samples of the parameter field. The model is trained without labeled solution data by enforcing geometry-aware constraints derived from variational energies, diffusion-based density equalization, and quasi-conformal theory. Experimental results on quasi-conformal mapping and density-equalizing mapping problems are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.
♻ ☆ How Much is Left? LLMs Linearly Encode Their Remaining Output Length NeurIPS 2026
Mohamed Amine Merzouk, Dmitri Carpov, Mirko Bronzi, Damiano Fornasiere, Adam Oberman
Large Language models generate tokens, without explicitly keeping track of the length of the generated text. This paper asks the question: can we estimate the number of tokens remaining in a generated response, using just a linear probe on the model's hidden states? Previous work on inference scheduling established that length is statistically predictable, using nonlinear methods. This paper contributes a linear representation method, using frozen hidden states of 7-8B instruction-tuned models, across seven datasets. We show that total completion length can be estimated, with performance stronger than statistical baselines, and stronger than the fair comparison to the prediction at the last token of the prompt. On the natural-language datasets, the probe's error lies between 0.57 and 0.88 of the statistical baseline's. Interestingly, when a retraction token occurs ("Wait"), the probe predicted length jumps upward by over 70 tokens, on average, compared to the baseline, where it drops by 0.7, on average. Moreover, the direction found can be used for length steering: adding to the probe direction increases completion length and vice-versa, on Llama-3.1-8B / GSM8K. These results indicate that LLMs have a linearly decodable internal representation of output length.
comment: NeurIPS 2026 camera-ready version. 19 pages, 6 figures. Code: https://github.com/mamerzouk/llm-output-length
♻ ☆ Conditional Flow Models Convert Epistemic Uncertainty into Apparent Aleatoric Variance
Navodita Sharma, Abhishek Shetty, Max Simchowitz, Pulkit Agrawal
Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly being used in place of deterministic predictors across machine learning, including for tasks that were classically formulated as regression. Given their success in such tasks, we ask the question: what useful information do the conditional distributions produced by CFMs carry beyond what a point predictor would provide? We identify a systematic phenomenon: in many natural regimes, CFM samples routinely have larger variance than the true conditional distribution, even in nearly deterministic regression problems. This effect is most pronounced where the model has not resolved the dependence on the conditioning variable, and thus the additional variance can be viewed as converting \emph{epistemic uncertainty} in fitting the ground truth conditional distribution into apparent \emph{aleatoric variance} in the generated samples. Through controlled synthetic and real-data experiments, and comparisons with explicit smoothing estimators, we show that the induced variance tracks model underfitting of complex or hard-to-fit targets, and decreases with additional training or data. We uncover surprising structure in this excess conditional variance that seems unique to CFMs and absent in the other standard probabilistic models that we test. We provide a theoretical account of the phenomenon in a simplified setting and demonstrate a consequent practical use-case of conditional flow-matching: designing high-coverage predictive sets that cover the ground-truth regression target.
♻ ☆ VirusCascade: Hijacking Collaborative Reflection in LLM-Powered Recommender Agents NDSS 2027
Yurong Hao, Wen Zhou, Guowei Guan, Tiantong Wu, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
Advancing beyond traditional static scoring models, LLM-powered agentic recommender systems (LLM-ARS) instantiate users and items as autonomous agents, whose semantic states are dynamically refined through a recurrent process known as collaborative reflection. While this mechanism improves recommendation quality, it simultaneously introduces a systemic vulnerability: adversarial evidence injected into a single agent can be rationalised into a legitimate preference narrative, written back into memory, and propagated to other agents through interaction contexts. We term the local rationalisation process reflection laundering, and its system-wide escalation through collaborative reflection collaborative-reflection hijacking. Existing attacks on recommender systems, whether based on interaction-level data poisoning or text-level adversarial perturbations, assume static pipelines and thus cannot exploit this recurrent, multi-agent amplification pathway. To bridge this gap, we first conduct a controlled vulnerability analysis that establishes two exploitable properties underlying collaborative-reflection hijacking: reflective persistence and cross-agent propagation. Then building on these findings, we propose VirusCascade, the first black-box targeted promotion attack that jointly shapes semantic and structural attack surfaces: the former ensures the target item is naturally rationalised as satisfying broad user preferences, the latter positions it for system-wide propagation. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets across diverse LLM-ARS architectures demonstrate that VirusCascade consistently achieves state-of-the-art targeted exposure under evaluated stealth constraints, reaching a mean E@20 of 0.384 and surpassing the strongest baseline by an absolute margin of +0.185.
comment: Accepted at NDSS 2027
♻ ☆ Caravan MultiMet: Extending Caravan with Multiple Weather Nowcasts and Forecasts
Guy Shalev, Frederik Kratzert
The Caravan large-sample hydrology dataset (Kratzert et al., 2023) was created to standardize and harmonize streamflow data from various regional datasets, combined with globally available meteorological forcing and catchment attributes. This community-driven project also allows researchers to conveniently extend the dataset for additional basins, as done 6 times to date (see https://github.com/kratzert/Caravan/discussions/10). We present a novel extension to Caravan, focusing on enriching the meteorological forcing data. Our extension adds three precipitation nowcast products (CPC, IMERG v07 Early, and CHIRPS) and three weather forecast products (ECMWF IFS HRES, GraphCast, and CHIRPS-GEFS) to the existing ERA5-Land reanalysis data. The inclusion of diverse data sources, particularly weather forecasts, enables more robust evaluation and benchmarking of hydrological models, especially for real-time forecasting scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, this extension makes Caravan the first large-sample hydrology dataset to incorporate weather forecast data, significantly enhancing its capabilities and fostering advancements in hydrological research, benchmarking, and real-time hydrologic forecasting. The data is publicly available under a CC-BY-4.0 license on Zenodo in two parts (https://zenodo.org/records/14161235, https://zenodo.org/records/14161281) and on Google Cloud Platform (GCP) - see more under the Data Availability chapter.
♻ ☆ ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
Philipp Mondorf, Adrien Deliège, Solim LeGris, Claas Beger, Ryan Yi, Barbara Plank, Brenden M. Lake, Todd M. Gureckis
Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.
comment: 38 pages, 24 figures
♻ ☆ Ostinato: Low-Latency CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents
Junning Zhu, Jianxiong Guo
Language-model agents increasingly run on local workstations with consumer GPUs, where quantized mixture-of-experts (MoE) models split routed experts between GPU and host memory. Prefix-cached agent sessions alternate single-token decode with short tool-return prefills, typically up to a few hundred tokens. Short tool turns touch more experts than consumer GPUs can hold, yet direct roughly 85% of DeepSeek-V4-Flash's routes to a static GPU pool while leaving 3.3-5.5 tokens per cold expert. Widely used local engines such as llama.cpp and KTransformers either copy tens of gigabytes over PCIe per turn, compute every route on the CPU while idling resident GPU experts, or budget GPU memory by whole layers and uniform per-layer quotas. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE engine that reuses one static cross-layer GPU pool in place across every forward pass. During decode and short tool turns, Ostinato computes resident routes on the GPUs and sparse cold routes on the CPU, so short turns copy no expert weights; on long prefills, it deduplicates cold uploads; and for multi-GPU decode, all-zero expert slots with device-side synchronization capture each GPU's decode step in one CUDA graph. Across held-out SWE and -bench sessions on three MoE models, Ostinato cuts median tool-turn waits by 2.5-6.6x and finishes sessions 1.36-3.83x faster than default baselines, staying 1.30-1.94x faster when baselines align their upload threshold and weight loading. It finishes sessions fastest across seven agent workloads, one to four GPUs, and up to eight concurrent sessions, while its cross-layer pool speeds up 335 GB DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.81-2.19x over llama.cpp's expert cache.
♻ ☆ Latent Diffusion for Internet of Things Attack Data Generation in Intrusion Detection
Estela Sánchez-Carballo, Francisco M. Melgarejo-Meseguer, José Luis Rojo-Álvarez
The growing deployment of IoT systems has increased the need for reliable intrusion detection under heterogeneous and imbalanced network traffic. However, representative malicious traffic, particularly for underrepresented attacks, remains difficult to obtain, while existing generative approaches do not consistently preserve distributional fidelity, multivariate dependencies, and coverage simultaneously. This work proposes LaDIS, an attack-specific framework that learns a mixed-type autoencoder representation and performs diffusion in an adaptive continuous latent space. LaDIS was compared with established adversarial, variational, and direct-space diffusion approaches across representative Flooding, Botnet, Recon, and Stealthy attacks using complementary measures of marginal and multivariate fidelity, dependency preservation, real--synthetic distinguishability, manifold structure, and computational efficiency. LaDIS provided a competitive balance across these dimensions, with particularly strong results for representative Botnet, Recon, and Stealthy attacks, while revealing an attack-dependent fidelity--coverage trade-off. Performing diffusion in latent space also reduced sampling time by approximately 3--5 times relative to direct-space diffusion, with negligible decoding overhead. Downstream utility was evaluated using TabNet and XGBoost, demonstrating that partial LaDIS augmentation consistently produced the best performance, increasing balanced accuracy from 0.86 to 0.94 for TabNet and from 0.92 to 0.96 for XGBoost, while improving the F1-score for low-volume attack families from 0.73 to 0.84 and from 0.82 to 0.88, respectively. These results show that attack-adaptive latent diffusion can generate structurally faithful attack traffic efficiently and, when used selectively, improve intrusion detection for underrepresented attacks.
comment: Revised version following peer review, with expanded experiments, additional generative baselines, latent dimensionality sensitivity analysis, and multiclass IDS validation. Submitted to IEEE. 16 pages, 3 figures
♻ ☆ Same behavior, different mechanism: what finite experiments can certify about how a network computes
Diaoxuan He, Linqian Wu, Chang Kong, Haoming Peng
Interpretability research, AI audits and assessments of machine consciousness make claims about how a system computes, not what it outputs. We give such claims a measurement theory. A claim is certifiable from finite interventions exactly when the mechanism lies at positive information distance from those that falsify it; it then costs at least log(1/alpha) over that distance, and an adaptive experiment attains this price asymptotically. Access, geometry and the logical form of the claim set the distance. In solvable networks, behavior carries no evidence about integrated information, and quantities that select one thing and report another have cliffs beside which cost grows as the inverse square of distance, whatever the margin. Equally accurate networks implement different circuits. In language models of up to 7.6 billion parameters, 220 of 223 audited claims about circuits, and a refusal mechanism, were certified on live interventions, 89% within the cost range registered beforehand.
comment: 54 pages, 6 main figures and 6 Extended Data figures. Substantially revised with a general certification framework, additional experiments on recurrent networks and language models, and an updated author list. Code and data are included as ancillary files
♻ ☆ Machine Learning-Driven Virtual Bidding with Electricity Market Efficiency Analysis
Yinglun Li, Nanpeng Yu, Wei Wang
This paper develops a machine learning-driven portfolio optimization framework for virtual bidding in electricity markets considering both risk constraint and price sensitivity. The algorithmic trading strategy is developed from the perspective of a proprietary trading firm to maximize profit. A recurrent neural network-based Locational Marginal Price (LMP) spread forecast model is developed by leveraging the inter-hour dependencies of the market clearing algorithm. The LMP spread sensitivity with respect to net virtual bids is modeled as a monotonic function with the proposed constrained gradient boosting tree. We leverage the proposed algorithmic virtual bid trading strategy to evaluate both the profitability of the virtual bid portfolio and the efficiency of U.S. wholesale electricity markets. The comprehensive empirical analysis on PJM, ISO-NE, and CAISO indicates that the proposed virtual bid portfolio optimization strategy considering the price sensitivity explicitly outperforms the one that neglects the price sensitivity. The Sharpe ratio of virtual bid portfolios for all three electricity markets are much higher than that of the S&P 500 index. It was also shown that the efficiency of CAISO's two-settlement system is lower than that of PJM and ISO-NE.
♻ ☆ Relative Discharge Stage Classification from Battery Sensor Measurements in Laboratory Discharge Tests
Khoa Tran, Tri Le, Hung-Cuong Trinh, Hung Tran-Nam
Relative discharge stage (RDS) is an ordinal target obtained by dividing the realized remaining discharge time by the total duration of the same discharge episode and assigning the ratio to a bin. We investigate whether these bins can be predicted from measurements available up to the present sample. The framework combines an electrothermal equivalent-circuit model and adaptive extended Kalman filter to estimate state of charge (SOC), then classifies discharge stage using the estimated SOC, current, terminal voltage, and surface temperature. With the evaluated two-layer convolutional network, the final-time prediction directly uses the three most recent observations. Earlier measurements can influence the output through the recursive SOC estimate. On complete discharge tests, the five-stage classifier achieved accuracies of 95.38% and 81.23% for FTP-75 and PDMHC and 76.41% and 73.87% for LCO_5 and LCO_6, respectively. These results characterize classification within the laboratory protocols. Incremental value over SOC alone, reference-based SOC accuracy, and utility in vehicle operation remain to be established.
♻ ☆ LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
Hanzhen Wang, Jiaming Xu, Guohao Dai
Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.
comment: 11 pages. Code and weights are available at the URL in the paper
♻ ☆ Manifold-Matching Autoencoders
Laurent Cheret, Vincent Létourneau, Isar Nejadgholi, Chris Drummond, Hussein Al Osman, Maia Fraser
Manipulating the structure of data in the latent space of an autoencoder is a long-standing goal of representation learning. We propose a simple regularization, Manifold Matching, that imposes an explicit geometric structure on that latent space. The idea is to take a reference representation R of the data, which need not be the raw input X fed to the network, and to minimize, batch-wise, the mean squared error between the pairwise distances in R and those in the latent space Z. Although the autoencoder still learns to reconstruct X, the shape of its latent space comes to mimic that of R. The objective requires no labels, only reference distances, and because those are scalars, the dimensionality of R is decoupled from that of Z: any reference can guide any bottleneck. Using this single instrument we study how different geometric structures can be imposed on a latent space, comparing against autoencoders built on geometric or topological regularizers. Across fifteen datasets under a shared protocol with statistical testing, the resulting Manifold-Matching Autoencoder (MMAE) matches the global-structure quality of persistence-based autoencoders, statistically tying RTD-AE on distance correlation and triplet accuracy, and stays competitive on the local and topological metrics that other methods lead, at the computational cost of a plain autoencoder: it uses only a batched distance loss, with no persistence computation. We frame MMAE not as a universal winner but as an efficient and controllable regularizer whose reference selects which structure the latent inherits, and which turns any fixed embedding into a reusable out-of-sample encoder. All experiments use a two-dimensional bottleneck.
comment: 32 pages, 10 figures. Code: https://github.com/laurent-cheret/manifold-matching-autoencoders
♻ ☆ A Geometric Perspective on Reward Function Updates in Inverse Reinforcement Learning NeurIPS 2026
Anish Diwan, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved using Lagrangian optimisation, by jointly optimising a primal-dual problem with gradient descent to obtain the optimal reward function parameters and corresponding optimal policy. While this algorithmic view of IRL has been highly influential, gradient-based reward updates only paint a partial picture, largely ignoring the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. In this paper, we present an occupancy-space view of reward updates in IRL. We leverage the insight that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, and show that the geometry along the e-geodesic (straight line in occupancy space) toward the optimal occupancy directly affects the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space. This perspective naturally suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. We show that this preconditioned gradient is just a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward, yielding efficient natural-gradient-style updates with little additional computational overhead. We then analyse these occupancy-space reward updates from a Mirror Descent (MD) perspective, and show that policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy. Finally, we conclude with convergence results of such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.
comment: Accepted as a conference paper at the The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
♻ ☆ Inferring Experimental Objectives in Microscopy Experiments from Decision Traces
Kamyar Barakati, Boris N. Slautin, Aditya Raghavan, Babita Babita, Surya Prakash Reddy, Jordan Marshall, Munireach Nannory, Stephen Puplampu, Alla Slautina, Faith M. Hines, Newsha Javanmardi, Sergei V. Kalinin
Modern microscopes can acquire, analyze and act on data far faster than human operators can decide what to measure next. Exploiting this speed in automated experiments requires the instrument to follow the scientific logic of the operator, and one way to encode that logic is through reward functions that become part of the operation process. Here we explore whether such reward functions can be learned from the decision histories of microscope operators. We propose multiple frameworks in which recorded choices among alternative measurement locations serve as comparative evidence about the operator's preferences, and we compare several algorithms for reconstructing the reward including interpretable linear models built on physically meaningful image descriptors, nonlinear functions of the same descriptors, an unsupervised image representation followed by preference modeling, and a preference trained deep kernel inspired model. The result of this analysis is a spatial field of reward functions over the sample that can be used to run the instrument. We also propose a way to benchmark these approaches, based on withheld decisions and on decision histories generated with known objectives. We then examine the possibility that a decision history contains changing priorities throughout the experiment. A hidden Markov model assigns distinct rewards to recurring selection strategies, whereas a continuous-state model tracks smoothly varying preference weights. Controlled sequences generated over real microscopy candidate sets show that both concealed switches and gradual drift can be recovered. These reward functions, learned directly from recorded decisions, provide candidate objectives for future automated microscopy experiments.
comment: 30 pages, 8 figures
♻ ☆ Reducing Fixed-Batch Client Idleness in Many-Client Edge Split Learning
Mohammad Kohankhaki, Valentin Rentschler, Carsten Kamp, Sigrid Brell-Cokcan, Anke Schmeink
Parallel Split Learning with Global Sampling (GPSL) trains a split model on a fixed-size batch drawn from the data of all clients. When the client population is much larger than the batch, most clients contribute no data in a round, and additional server capacity does not change this. We propose Global Clustered Parallel Split Learning (GCPSL), which assigns clients to stable clusters, runs one GPSL workload per cluster concurrently, and periodically fuses the split-model replicas. We derive the expected direct data participation under the batch sampler, which separates repeated sampling of the same clients from idling at the fusion barrier. With 256 clients, more clusters raise participation but reduce the client diversity seen by each workload. In three paired runs on four H100 GPUs, GCPSL raises direct data participation from 22% to 57-60%. With random or size-balanced clusters, it reaches 85% CIFAR-10 validation accuracy in 5.7 minutes, 1.6 times faster than GPSL with its batch sharded across the same GPUs. It matches per-step synchronized data-parallel GPSL at 85% and reaches 88% in about 10 instead of 19.5 minutes, without per-step global gradient or BatchNorm synchronization. Concurrent execution is 3.11 times faster than sequential execution of the same workloads.
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Extended version of v1 under a new title, with two additional authors. ♻ ☆ Neural Isomorphic Fields: A Transformer-based Algebraic Numerical Embedding
Hamidreza Sadeghi, Saeedeh Momtazi, Reza Safabakhsh
Neural network models often face challenges when processing very small or very large numbers due to issues such as overflow, underflow, and unstable output variations. To mitigate these problems, we propose using embedding vectors for numbers instead of directly using their raw values. These embeddings aim to retain essential algebraic properties while preventing numerical instabilities. We introduce Neural Isomorphic Fields (NIF), a digit-sequence Transformer autoencoder trained with two learned commutative operators and an antisymmetric neural comparator. At zero loss, the embeddings provably form an ordered integral domain isomorphic to the decimal fractions, whose field of fractions is isomorphic to the rationals. For the trained model, we bound errors of operations, chains and algebraic laws by decoding margins, defects and Lipschitz constants. Trained on up to 25 digits, NIF reaches at least 99.9% exact match on closure, identity, associativity and distributivity and 99.8% on ten-step chains and the order relation. With four channels per decimal place, reconstruction and both operations exceed 99.7% exact match on numbers of up to 200 digits whose parts stay within training lengths, so the dimension grows linearly. In a language model, frozen operators raise exact match on 14-20-digit word problems from 12.0% (operators off) to 39.7%.
♻ ☆ How to Enhance Downstream Adversarial Robustness (almost) without Touching the Pre-Trained Foundation Model?
Meiqi Liu, Zhuoqun Huang, Hongbo Li, Young-geun Kim, Yue Xing
With the rise of powerful foundation models, a pre-training-fine-tuning paradigm becomes increasingly popular these days: A foundation model is pre-trained using a huge amount of data from various sources, and then the downstream users only need to fine-tune and adapt it to specific downstream tasks. However, due to the high computation complexity of adversarial training, it is not feasible to fine-tune the foundation model to improve its robustness on the downstream task. Observing the above challenge, we want to improve the downstream robustness without updating/accessing the weights in the foundation model. Inspired from existing literature in robustness inheritance (Kim et al., 2020), through theoretical investigation, we identify a close relationship between robust contrastive learning with the adversarial robustness of supervised learning. To further validate and utilize this theoretical insight, we design a simple-yet-effective robust auto-encoder as a data pre-processing method before feeding the data into the foundation model. The proposed approach has zero access to the foundation model when training the robust auto-encoder. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving the robustness of downstream tasks, verifying the connection between the feature robustness (implied by small adversarial contrastive loss) and the robustness of the downstream task.

♻ ☆ When does off-block Hessian curvature help an optimization step?
Maxim Bolshim, Alexander Kugaevskikh
Testing an off-block Hessian correction alone can discard a step that lowers minibatch loss. We measure both the missed improvement and the gain from rescaling the remaining correction. A reference based on diagonal-block norms distinguishes changes in the diagonal profile during training from changes in relative off-block mass. This reference sharply bounds the off-block fraction for positive semidefinite matrices. Regrouping fixed ResNet-18 weights from stages to layers takes the estimated fraction from below to above its partition-specific bound in all six CIFAR-100 comparisons under a conditional probe screen. At nine ResNet-50 checkpoints on Stanford Cars, we measure the off-block contribution to the linearized gradient change along a K-FAC step. At four base-step endpoints, predicted and measured slopes along the original correction have opposite signs. Each subspace draw (two per checkpoint) supplies one Hessian-informed map for the off-block residual, the remainder and their sum. At unit scale before acceptance, the off-block correction alone worsens the base in 17/18 comparisons; the combination beats the remainder in ten, including nine of those 17. At one checkpoint only the combination improves on the base in both draws. Matching correction norms reverses seven of the ten preferences, including both at that checkpoint.

♻ ☆ Click and Count: Multimodal Prototype Adaptation for Class-Agnostic Object Counting SC
Amani Aifi, Wassim Bouachir, Ahmed Zgaren, Nizar Bouguila
We propose a multimodal, class-agnostic, density-based object counting framework that specifies the object of interest through visual exemplars, a text description, or both, within a single iterative refinement pipeline. Existing counters typically fall into two groups: methods that fuse two modalities, a hand-drawn bounding box and a text description, to specify the target object, and single-modality methods that rely on either a box exemplar or text alone. A few recent methods replace the box with a point or click. We expand a single click into a precise object mask via a frozen visual-prompt segmentation model, feeding an iterative prototype-refinement process that also fuses a text description at every refinement step. We make two contributions: first, a click-derived exemplar extraction module that removes the bounding-box requirement of prior exemplar-based counters; second, a per-step text-fusion mechanism that combines visual and textual prompts throughout refinement. Combined with text guidance, our model achieves state-of-the-art counting accuracy, outperforming prior click-based counting methods across all metrics and surpassing the box-exemplar base architecture in mean absolute error. The code is available at github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count.
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2027 IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (IEEE SSCI 2027). Code: https://github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count
♻ ☆ Escaping Latent Traps by Remembering: Training-Free Episodic Kernel Repulsion for World-Model Planning
Yican Zhao, Bolin Yang, Ruizhe Wang, Haiyang Guo, Fuji Yang, Bingo Wing-Kuen Ling, Zelin Zang
Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. Because this distance is not geodesic, it creates latent traps---local minima or flat basins behind walls, at corners and in dead ends---where memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free, test-time cost term that penalises candidate plans via a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, normalised by the current batch base cost so a single strength transfers across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR improves success in all eight settings without changing the model, planner or search budget, matching or exceeding $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute in seven of eight settings while adding $\sim 25$ ms ($<1\%$) per replan. Controlled trap-fork interventions confirm that the memory causes escape, and an untuned configuration transfers directly to DINO-WM with CEM (e.g. $44.7\%\to 100.0\%$ on long PointMaze, $+19.3$ points on long Wall) and to JEPA-WM on Metaworld mw-reach-wall ($25.3\%\to 40.7\%$).
comment: 29 pages, including references and appendix
♻ ☆ SVDP: Training-Free Contextual Sparsity Predictors for Fast LLM Inference
Georgii Serbin, Kirill Koshkin, Zhongao Sun, Anastasiya Bistrigova, C. C. Korikov
Contextual sparsity is one of the approaches used to reduce computational complexity in the inference process of large language models (LLMs). Existing techniques for efficient LLM inference acceleration based on contextual sparsity with minimal accuracy degradation require training sparse pattern predictors. This paper presents a framework for accelerating inference of ReGLU-based feed-forward networks (FFNs) within LLMs. The proposed framework provides a fast, training-free method for building sparse pattern predictors using truncation-aware singular value decomposition (SVD) of the gate projection matrix, along with a threshold calibration algorithm, and inference executors supporting conditional computation on CUDA and CANN devices. Experiments on three sparse LLMs with an average activation sparsity level of 90% in the FFNs demonstrate up to a 1.8x reduction in end-to-end decoding time while maintaining less than 1% degradation in benchmark scores on tasks involving complex math and code generation. This work advances the deployment of LLMs on edge devices.
♻ ☆ SparseHPS: A Unified Model for Human Pose and Shape Estimation across Depth Cameras and LiDARs
Ilya Zaychuk
Recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds is central to motion capture, robotics and self-driving vehicles, because depth cameras and LiDARs sense a person directly in metric 3D and work under any lighting. However, current approaches are each tailored to one sensor type: point density differs by more than ten times between devices, public datasets are labeled with incompatible body models, and LiDAR approaches need long input sequences to offset sparse scans. In this work, we present SparseHPS, a novel sensor-agnostic network that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global translation from a human point cloud with one set of weights, for single frames and streams alike. Specifically, SparseHPS encodes the cloud with a LitePT backbone over sparse voxels, represents every joint by a learnable query decoded with one common head, localizes the body by voting over voxels, and draws temporal context from a causal memory of tokens from the seven preceding frames. A single model is trained on ten datasets that mix rendered clouds with real depth-camera and LiDAR captures, all converted to one body model. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the SLOPER4D and FreeMotion LiDAR benchmarks, where SparseHPS lowers the root-relative joint error by 22% and 11%, respectively, compared with the strongest prior method, which needs 32 frames. On real Azure Kinect captures of held-out HuMMan subjects, SparseHPS attains a joint error of 34.7 mm. Moreover, the current frame alone already yields the bulk of this accuracy.
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://ghostlate.github.io/SparseHPS
♻ ☆ Regret-Oracle Complexity Tradeoffs in Agnostic Online Learning
Idan Attias, Steve Hanneke, Arvind Ramaswami
Agnostic online learning is classically solved via a reduction to the realizable setting, utilizing Littlestone's Standard Optimal Algorithm (SOA) as a base learner. However, the SOA can be computationally intractable to implement even for a single round. To overcome this barrier, recent work in oracle-efficient online learning replaces the SOA with a realizable base learner that accesses the concept class exclusively through an offline empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. While such agnostic learners achieve expected regret $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt{T\cdot 2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$, which is near-optimal in the horizon $T$ for fixed Littlestone dimension $d_{\mathrm{LD}}$, they require $\mathcal{O}\big(T^{2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$ oracle calls. In this work, we significantly improve this oracle complexity while relying on an even weaker primitive: a weak-consistency oracle, which merely decides whether a given labeled dataset is realizable. At the core of our approach is an adaptive and dynamic agnostic-to-realizable reduction that actively prunes non-realizable label sequences on the fly. By using the VC dimension ($d_{\mathrm{VC}}$) to bound the number of dynamically maintained active paths, our algorithm reduces the total query complexity down to $\mathcal{O}(T^{d_{\mathrm{VC}}+1})$ while perfectly preserving near-optimal expected regret. Crucially, this dynamic pruning also yields a memory reduction over the standard reduction. Furthermore, we formally quantify the regret--oracle complexity tradeoff, providing upper bounds that smoothly interpolate between restricted query budgets and attainable expected regret. We complement these with lower bounds proving that any learner restricted to $Q = o(\sqrt{T})$ queries must suffer an expected regret of $Ω(T/Q)$.
♻ ☆ Distributional Deep Hedging
El-Amine Cherrat, Skander Kazdaghli, Iordanis Kerenidis
Deep hedging learns a hedging strategy by optimising a risk preference over a neural-network policy. The preference is fixed before training, so each new preference requires a new policy and, in actor-critic methods, a new critic. We propose distributional deep hedging, in which the distribution of the hedging profit and loss is learned through its quantiles and the risk preference is applied afterwards, as a weight on those quantiles. We characterise the preferences that admit this representation, which include expected shortfall and its mixtures, and show that the entropic utility is computed from the same quantiles. At the current policy, each of these preferences is bounded below by an expected utility with the same gradient. This bound reduces risk-sensitive hedging to a sequence of risk-neutral problems, from which we derive policy-search and actor-critic algorithms. In numerical experiments, the learned hedges approach references computed by dynamic programming, and a single distributional critic trained without a preference can serve preferences chosen after training.
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables; v2: introduction clarified, references added
♻ ☆ Anti-Collapse Dynamics and the Emergence of Multi-Time-Scale Learning in Recurrent Neural Networks
Lorenzo Livi
Long-range learning is hard for recurrent networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, because the influence of a past input fades with the lag $\ell$, and if it fades too fast the dependence cannot be learned from finite data. This fade is captured by an envelope $f(\ell)$. An exponential fade makes the data needed to learn a lag-$\ell$ dependence grow exponentially, putting long horizons out of reach; a power-law fade keeps the cost polynomial. We show that the asymptotic decay behavior of $f(\ell)$ is not fixed by the architecture. Instead, it emerges from the coupling between the state dynamics and parameter dynamics, settling into either a collapsed regime (fast, exponential forgetting) or an extended, anti-collapsed regime (slow, power-law forgetting). The intuition is a competition within these coupled dynamics. The systematic part of the training updates pulls long effective time scales back toward the network's typical range, while rare, heavy-tailed fluctuations can push a few far beyond it. When these pushes are strong enough to balance the pull, the extended regime survives. We make this mathematically precise with a coarse-grained stochastic process and derive the explicit threshold above which this balance holds. A single exponent, the spectral exponent~$β$, then governs both the spread of time scales and how slowly the network forgets. Realizing the regime in practice needs one more ingredient: the joint action of the architecture and the optimizer must be able to hold such a broad spread. A network whose capacity to generate broad time-scale spectra is severely constrained still collapses, even when supplied with strong heavy-tailed forcing. Heavy-tailed fluctuations thus act not as noise to be suppressed, but as the mechanism that sustains long-range learning.
comment: Revised the phase classification below the jump-amplitude threshold and derived the corresponding stationary time-scale tail and envelope decay
♻ ☆ In- and Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs for Simple Visual Planning Tasks
Yannic Neuhaus, Chanoknan Tanchotikul, Nicolas Flammarion, Matthias Hein, Francesco Croce
Integrating reasoning in (multimodal) large language models has recently led to significant improvement of their capabilities. However, generalization in reasoning models is still vaguely defined and poorly understood. In this work, we present an evaluation framework to rigorously examine how well chain-of-thought (CoT) approaches generalize in simple visual planning, specifically on a grid-based navigation task. The versatility of the task and its data allows us to fine-tune model variants using different input representations (visual and textual) and CoT reasoning strategies, and systematically evaluate them under both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) test conditions. Our experiments show that the out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., to larger maps) is largely impacted by the format used for input maps and CoT chains. Surprisingly, we find that coordinate-based reasoning traces which combine text descriptions yield the best OOD generalization. Moreover, CoT reproducing the steps of the A* algorithm yields the state-of-the-art ID accuracy, and simple augmentation of the map solutions seen during training greatly boosts OOD results. Repeating the experiments with maps represented by coordinates yields similar results for another model family. Tests on structurally complex maps reveal a sharp performance drop when shortest solutions require many movement directions or turns. Additional fine-tuning on examples of directionally complex maps substantially recovers this performance. Finally, purely text-based models consistently outperform those utilizing image-based inputs, including a recently proposed approach relying on latent space reasoning.
♻ ☆ Mechanism-Based Intelligence: Differentiable Incentives for Rational Coordination and Equilibrium Alignment in Multi-Agent Systems
Stefano Grassi
Autonomous multi-agent systems struggle with the Hayekian Information problem (using dispersed private knowledge) and the Hurwiczian Incentive problem (aligning local actions with global objectives). I introduce Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), an architecture that treats intelligence as emergent from the coordination of specialized modules rather than a single monolithic model. At its core, the Differentiable Price Mechanism computes the exact gradient of the system loss as a price; subtracting its own marginal cost, each agent obtains the incentive signal $$\mathbf{G}_i = - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i},$$ and the transfers take the Groves form. Each agent's best response minimizes the global loss given the actions of others, so the negative global loss is an exact potential for the resulting game, with a unique equilibrium at the global optimum. Gradient-based play converges to it under a step-size condition when effort is costless, and stops near it otherwise: a satisficing rule halts each agent's search when its marginal gain no longer exceeds its marginal computational cost. The equilibrium requires no knowledge of agents' private costs, so asymmetric information causes no welfare loss; simultaneous gradient dynamics require only a public bound on cost curvature. Each iteration scales linearly ($\mathcal{O}(N)$) with the number of agents, though for losses summed over agents the iteration count also grows with $N$. For known, differentiable losses, MBI avoids the combinatorial search of Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. Under convexity and smoothness conditions, MBI aligns agent self-interest with the Planner's objective, offering an auditable approach to multi-agent coordination.
comment: v2: substantially revised, new title. Groves-form transfers; exact potential game; Planner prices only the system loss; convergence of simultaneous updates with satisficing stop; limitations stated; related work added. ♻ ☆ Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds NeurIPS 2026
Lucas Ng, Georgios Batzolis, Mark Girolami
On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recent extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We derive a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error by a residual term that vanishes under compatibility. On compact manifolds, we show that existing compatible objectives put density on infeasible velocities. To tackle both issues, we propose an exponential family over endpoints with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. In practice, and with low overhead, this reduces to a reweighting of the flow matching loss. On spaces of constant curvature, this treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Compared to prior art, our method finds the correct velocities on the test case, outperforms in general on high-dimensional product tori, and, for two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere, achieves substantial NLL improvements. When evaluated on a large dataset of human poses, our method surpasses prior work according to sample-based metrics.
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
♻ ☆ Fixed Points and Envelope Dynamics on Credal Hyperspaces
Michele Caprio, Mengqi Chen, Siu Lun Chau, Krikamol Muandet
Let $X$ be a compact metric space and consider the hyperspace $\mathscr C_X$ of nonempty weakly closed convex sets of Borel probability measures on $X$, called credal sets. These sets represent uncertainty about which probability law governs the phenomenon of interest. We equip $\mathscr C_X$ with the Hausdorff metric induced by a metric for weak convergence. Credal order intervals $[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}] = \{ \mathcal{P}\in\mathscr C_X: \mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{B} \}$ are complete lattices, and every inclusion-monotone, Hausdorff-continuous self map of such an interval has least and greatest fixed points obtained as limits of iteration from $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$. For families of inclusion-monotone updates that may vary with time, we construct lower and upper envelope maps that bound every admissible trajectory. When these envelope maps are Hausdorff-continuous, the distance of every trajectory from a limiting credal interval vanishes uniformly over all switching sequences and initial credal sets. Coalescence of the limiting interval endpoints yields convergence to a common credal limit. We then construct the credal evolution induced by a time consistent Nisio semigroup. Uniform $W_1$ contraction of the underlying Markov semigroups induces Hausdorff-Wasserstein contraction of the credal evolution, yielding a unique common invariant credal set, exponential convergence from every initial credal set, and a support functional equal to the robust ergodic limit. We also derive perturbation bounds from finite time Nisio discrepancies and one step kernel set discrepancies, and characterize the countable sequences of support coordinates that represent credal sets, providing an explicit reconstruction formula.
♻ ☆ Biologically Inspired Coordination of Parameter Selection and Update Strength for Language Model Adaptation
Xiao Zhang, Tianyu Hu, Juntao Lyu, Qianchuan Zhao, Huimin Ma
Adapting a source-trained language model to a target task requires deciding which parameters to update and how strongly when learning signals are uncertain. We introduce Synapse Consolidation (SyCo), a biologically inspired framework that coordinates these two controls. Rac1-associated forgetting and memory-trace redistribution motivate retaining selected source-derived low-rank components while resetting others for target adaptation. MAPK-associated signal processing motivates combining multiple prediction-based indicators over time to regulate update strength. SyCo combines these controls with a structured consistency objective and a small, fixed buffer of labelled source examples. Target labels are not used during adaptation. We evaluate the framework in Multi-source Open-set Adaptation (MOA), using source-initialized target learners for tasks absent from source training and for perturbed held-out inputs from source tasks. These results show how coordinated control of update location and strength can improve target adaptation under uncertain learning signals.

We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. ♻ ☆ Protecting Confidentiality, Privacy and Integrity in Collaborative Learning
Dong Chen, Alice Dethise, Istemi Ekin Akkus, Ivica Rimac, Antti Koskela, Marco Canini, Wei Wang, Ruichuan Chen
A collaboration between dataset owners and model owners is needed for effective machine learning (ML) training. During this collaboration, however, dataset owners and model owners want to protect the confidentiality of their respective assets (i.e., datasets, models and training code), with the dataset owners also caring about the privacy of individual users whose data is in the datasets. Existing solutions provide limited confidentiality for models and training code, suffer from data privacy issues, or incur unacceptable performance. Specifically, Citadel++ takes a chained approach. First, we employ the Virtual Machine-level Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) as the training runtime to provide confidentiality protections for datasets, model and training code. Second, we create a privacy barrier that improves upon differential privacy techniques to safeguard the privacy of individual user data while maintaining model utility. Third, we construct and optimize a Virtual Machine Privilege Level (VMPL)-enforced fine-grained sandbox to regulate the dataflow in the system to ensure that our privacy barrier is always applied even when the model and training code maybe maliciously designed. Finally, we employ specific TEE capabilities to ensure the integrity of our privacy barrier and sandboxing mechanisms for their correct execution. To our knowledge, Citadel++ is the first collaborative training system providing strong confidentiality and privacy protections for dataset owners and model owners simultaneously. We analyze Citadel++ security properties and implement a full prototype. Our evaluation shows that Citadel++ provides strong guarantees with modest overheads.

At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. ☆ PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation

The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory. To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner. We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.

We hypothesize that targeting a single conceptual ability has little support, since the first-order abilities it would have to reach are often partially idiosyncratic and not identifiable in practice. This would mean that, from public benchmark scores alone, general intelligence is hard to define, identify, and target as a single construct in language model development. Future experiments should run training regimes that target both theoretically abstract general ability and tasks with semantic similarity and examine how abilities transfer across test sets of diverse formats.

While Rust is often claimed to match C's performance, runtime safety checks, compiler optimizations, and hardware microarchitecture interact in ways that complicate performance diagnosis. Across 8 of the 12 benchmarks, at least one Rust implementation performs within 10% of its C counterpart or outperforms it. Guided by these diagnoses, we develop an LLVM compiler pass that hoists redundant bounds checks through guarded loop versioning while preserving Rust's panic behavior. The pass enables downstream compiler optimizations, including loop unrolling and conditional-move conversion, reducing Selection Sort's overhead from 2.95x to 1.00x and improving Merge Sort from 1.43x to 0.91x relative to C. One researcher's unblinded review of 15 randomly sampled sessions found all scores reasonable and explanations supported. In a controlled scenario, we injected context defects into one data-analysis task and ran it twelve times. Every defect condition used more tokens than the clean baseline (mean +91%), and five evaluator models flagged 50-85% of targeted dimensions and 14-36% of non-targeted dimensions. Fidelity defects were detected most consistently and Actionability defects least. Because interventions were imperfectly isolated, these results are exploratory. All 15 scaffolded labs shared seven elements: input-processing-output (IPO) reasoning, instructor-guided programming, an independent task, a Google Colab/Gradio extension, debugging support, a task checklist, and submission requirements. Because student learning outcomes were not examined, we make no claims about instructional effectiveness. Instead, the paper offers a transparent design precedent and identifies priorities for future empirical evaluation. When consumption rises after a change, the team cannot tell whether the increase is worth investigating, worth accepting, or neither. A change to tracing, retries or a shared component can affect consumption far beyond the modified component. This thesis asks how energy objectives can become actionable engineering instruments rather than reporting metrics. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) answered a similar question for reliability with service-level indicators, objectives and response policies. We take SRE as the guiding research vision and study where the analogy holds for energy and where it breaks. An energy objective could, for example, bound the energy per successful transaction under stated workload conditions. The thesis connects three threads into one experimentally evaluated methodology. Useful-work semantics define what a successful transaction is. Energy attribution assigns shared and auxiliary consumption to transactions. Service-level engineering decisions act on the resulting energy objectives. Existing work covers attribution methods, measurement frameworks and sustainability objectives, mostly at component level and without a link to decisions. Our prior work on service-level energy modeling showed that the energy of auxiliary services is often overlooked and hard to measure. Planned experiments compare aggregate, request-normalized and useful-work-based indicators under controlled changes to observability configuration and injected failures. Whether transaction-level attribution is needed for these decisions, or whether service-level attribution with outcome counts is sufficient, is an open question the experiments are designed to answer.

On TOGBench, target selection, SE limitations, and property validation restrict validated properties to 2.8% of all methods. The resulting mean mutation score of 48.6% falls below the 50.9% of EvoSuite and the 51.1% of Teralizer. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost. We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. This study argues that fairness in artificial intelligence systems cannot be achieved by focusing solely on their technical aspects, necessitating a holistic approach. This study employs a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 applies computational content analysis to 360 occupational narratives generated by ChatGPT across four countries (Canada, Germany, India, and Bangladesh) using gender-neutral prompts to examine whether professions are predominantly associated with one gender and whether these patterns remain consistent across regions. Phase 2 examines the extent to which students recognize potential bias in AI, their trust in AI for consequential decision-making, and how these perceptions relate to themes in EDI and AI ethics scholarship. By combining output-level bias analysis with user perception data, this study identifies the empirical foundations necessary for future EDI-AI co-design frameworks, outlining the sociotechnical dimensions that such frameworks must address to be effective.
☆ Found in Translation: Five Entry Points to Translate AI Literacy Frameworks in the Design of Educational Materials
Luis Morales-Navarro, Karl-Emil K. Bilstrup, Mille Skovhus Lunding, Luke Connelly, Ane V. Jensen, Maja Dybboe, Yasmin B. Kafai, Marianne Graves Petersen, Ole Sejer Iversen
While there is a plethora of AI literacy and informatics frameworks, in practice it is difficult for designers of educational materials and educators to decide where to start and how to use these in learning activities. At the same time, recent reviews show that despite the fact that most frameworks emphasize the socio-technical nature of AI, in practice interventions tend to center on preparing learners to use AI. To address these issues, we ask: How can multiple stakeholders negotiate and translate AI literacy framework ideas into common language that can be used to design introductory learning materials for primary school children, teachers and parents? We present three vignettes that illustrate how the entry points were generative in the design of learning activities, learning tools and media content for school and home. This paper contributes an account of the participatory development of five entry points that serve as generative and negotiable resources for designing educational materials.
☆ Protective-Design Pre-Emption in Child-Facing Generative AI NeurIPS 2026
Verena Jasmin Hallitschke, Mahelie Dissanayake, Elisa Nguyen
Generative AI is adopted rapidly by children, yet unrestricted general-audience models dominate their usage. This paper presents the open problem of \emph{protective-design pre-emption}: Delayed market introduction, low access thresholds, utility gaps, habituation, and peer adoption foster unrestricted AI model lock-in, leading children to bypass child-centric platforms. With first signs of lower adoption of child-centric platforms, we argue that this shift may reinforce existing AI risks such as exposing children to deepened parasocial dependencies, skill erosion, and misinformation. To address this problem, we propose interdisciplinary research directions to quantify pre-emption, understand its socio-technical drivers, and develop interventions ensuring child-centric AI is actively adopted, not just available.
comment: Accepted for NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI
☆ Blaming the Machine, Billing the Victim? How Mock Jurors Reassign Fault from Generative AI Systems and Respond to Liability Cliffs in Tort
Tin Trung Nguyen, Jiannan Xu, Bao Kham Chau, Hal Daumé, Zubin Jelveh
Generative AI complicates tort liability attribution when people blame a generative AI system that cannot itself bear legally relevant fault. We investigate where this blame goes when fault must be allocated among legal persons, and whether American discontinuous apportionment doctrines influence mock jurors' factual findings of fault. Such doctrines include Contributory negligence, Joint and several liability, and their 50% or 51% variations, all of which have a fault-percentage threshold or a "cliff" where the victim-entitled compensation (or a defendant's liability) jumps to zero (or to all compensatory damages). Our pre-registered human subjects experiment (N=199 Prolific participants) shows that as many U.S. mock jurors (36%) blame the AI system itself, the AI blame often "leaks" to the victim or to the AI user (in 27% to 73% of our AI-blaming records, depending on how leakage is calculated). Although mock jurors rarely change their blame assignment from one side of the liability cliff to the other, these participants do not acknowledge the legal doctrine or its monetary consequence when explaining their changes. Our empirical results illustrate how a narrow doctrinal exception in tort, carving out "joint and several liability" for those deploying or using Generative AI without reasonable care, might mitigate the impact of blame leakage on victims' deserved compensation without introducing significant jury nullification risks.

☆ MyMuse: A Personal Museum for Post-Visit Inquiry and Reflection
Jiyeon Bae, Chunggi Lee, Jinwook Seo, Hanspeter Pfister
Artwork photographs may preserve what visitors saw without preserving why it mattered. Revisiting them can involve recalling earlier responses and developing new questions and interpretations as knowledge and personal experiences change. Yet recurring interests may remain difficult to recognize across individual exchanges. Informed by a formative study with ten visitors, we present MyMuse, a post-visit system that connects inquiry about individual artworks with reflection across visitors' accumulated records. In its Personal Museum, visitors revisit artworks, ask questions, and record interpretations that inform subsequent system responses. Its interactive Narrative Report reorganizes the same records across artworks through four interpretive lenses. In two within-subject studies with 16 participants, direct comparisons favored MyMuse for vivid revisitation. The report received higher ratings for recurring-interest awareness, cross-artwork connections, and unexpected discovery than a per-artwork presentation of the same records. These findings suggest that examining accumulated records can support reflection on recurring interests and relationships among visitors' responses across artworks.
