☆ "What Should I Do?" Guidelines for Responsibly Integrating AI in Software Engineering
Rudrajit Choudhuri, Fatima A. Moussaoui, Carmen Badea, Christian Bird, Jenna L. Butler, Brian Houck, Margaret Burnett, Anita Sarma
Speculations abound about the "right" ways for developers to integrate AI into their software engineering (SE) work, but the evidence that exists is sparse and contradictory. Yet, developers are held responsible for the products they ship with (or without) AI's help, so they need to integrate AI in responsible ways. To address this gap, we conducted a two-phase, large-scale investigation with 1,118 developers at Microsoft, GitHub, and Pfizer. In Phase 1, we surveyed 860 developers at Microsoft on where they sought and resisted AI support in their daily work, and from their accounts, synthesized 35 developer-facing guidelines: 29 across five categories of SE work and 6 cross-cutting ones. A year later, as AI capabilities and developers' experiences co-evolved, we validated them in Phase 2 with 258 developers in technology (Microsoft, GitHub) and biopharmaceutical (Pfizer) domains. Developers in our study found the guidelines clearly worded (92%) and relevant to their work (91%), and most wanted to adopt them in their own work (89%). We also report how developers described operationalizing these guidelines in practice: using AI to refine their craft and delegate verifiable work, while keeping judgment and accountability for themselves. For relationship-centric work, endorsement varied with developers' domain and their SE and AI experience. Overall, we offer concrete advice from in-the-trenches developers to other in-the-trenches developers, and a shared vocabulary that engineering teams can adopt to integrate AI well in their work.
☆ Micro Operational Robustness of LLMs on Code Generation
Debalina Ghosh Paul, Hong Zhu, Ian Bayley
It is now common practice in software development for large language models (LLMs) to be used to generate program code. It is desirable to evaluate the robustness of LLMs for this usage. This paper is concerned in particular with how sensitive LLMs are to variations in descriptions of the coding tasks. However, existing techniques for evaluating this robustness are unsuitable for code generation because the input data space of natural language (NL) descriptions is discrete and sparse. To address this problem, we propose a robustness evaluation method called scenario domain analysis, which aims to find the expected minimal change in the NL descriptions of coding tasks that would cause the LLMs to produce incorrect outputs. We have formally proved the theoretical properties of the method and also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of four state-of-the-art LLMs: Gemini-pro, Codex, Llamma2 and Falcon 7B, and have found that we are able to rank these with confidence from best to worst. Moreover, we have also studied how robustness varies in different scenarios, including the variations with the topic of the coding task and with the complexity of its sample solution, and found that robustness is lower for more complex tasks and also lower for more advanced topics, such as multi-threading and data structures.
☆ Refined, Reliable and Reproducible: Algorithmic Analysis and Reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder
Alvaro Roy Schachner, Dante Javier Paz, Juan Antonio Rico Gallego, Carlos Mauricio Correa, Andrés Nicolás Ruiz, Sebastián Rogelio Gualpa, Juan Bautista Cabral
Cosmic voids are vast underdense regions of the Universe that encode valuable information about its large-scale structure and evolution. By extending spherical voids into overlapping sphere structures, the Popcorn Void Finder demonstrated an improved statistical characterization of cosmic void populations. However, its origin as a research prototype progressively hindered its maintainability and extensibility. Moreover, post-publication algorithmic modifications have not been systematically evaluated, leaving their statistical and computational consequences insufficiently characterized. In this work, we present a comprehensive reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder, prioritizing algorithmic transparency, maintainability, and reproducibility. We document the complete identification procedure, revisit the original algorithmic choices, and evaluate their statistical and computational consequences. Comparisons between implementations revealed a significant change in the behavior of the Void Size Function, which is now characterized by a power-law regime transitioning to a Schechter-like distribution. These changes not only provide a better characterization of void sizes, but enable a new and more robust method to the determination of the shot-noise dominated regime, without implicit dependencies on internal finder parameters present in previous works. Performance benchmarks demonstrate a 1.62x speedup in spherical void identification and a substantial improvement in overlap-removal throughput. We determined the Popcorn algorithm to be negatively affected by load imbalance, and found a speedup of 63x in a tested configuration with a newly introduced early growth termination criterion. These results establish a more maintainable and reproducible foundation for popcorn void identification, while clarifying the statistical and computational trade-offs that govern its performance.
☆ CivilCADBench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Understanding, Reconstructing, and Designing Civil Engineering Drawing Sets
Zelin Zheng, Difei Wu, Xinyan Liu, Minghong Chen, Antoni B. Chan, Difan Zou
Civil infrastructure is designed, built, and maintained through engineering drawing sets, yet preparing and revising them remains labour-intensive and calls for automation. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are promising candidates, but assessing them requires a benchmark grounded in real engineering practice. We introduce CivilCADBench, a benchmark for understanding, reconstructing, and designing civil engineering drawing sets, built from real infrastructure drawings and source CAD files containing over 250,000 CAD entities. Unlike parametric 3D CAD models, these drawings are dense, layered, and multi-sheet; and since prints are lossy projections with no pixel trace of layers, a file can print correctly yet remain wrongly organised. CivilCADBench comprises three task families of increasing difficulty: understanding tasks are evaluated with 2,183 expert-reviewed questions ranging from single sheets to whole sets, while reconstruction and design tasks are agentic, requiring models to rebuild printed pages as editable CAD files, either as single pages or entire drawing sets, and to produce new designs. These tasks are performed across 232 pages, 28 sets, and 19 design tasks, and evaluated by a deterministic scorer that compares model outputs with the designers' source files on geometry, layers, text, and dimensions. We evaluate seven frontier MLLMs on CivilCADBench, and find that they read and redraw printed content accurately but recover the file structure poorly: the best model scores above 90% in understanding and single-page reconstruction, yet only 60% on layer assignment and 48% on design. Grounded in real engineering practice, CivilCADBench exposes both the capabilities and the limitations of frontier models in professional civil engineering, laying a foundation for next-generation models and agentic systems for intelligent civil engineering.

☆ Dhaani: A Data-Flow-Driven Tool for Greenfield Construction and Brownfield Modernisation
Shraddha Surana, Ashwin Srinivasan
Large language models can generate plausible code quickly, but an end-to-end prompt leaves developers with little control over decomposition, interfaces, or the assumptions that must survive later revisions. We present Dhaani, a free desktop application for greenfield program construction and brownfield repository modernisation. It makes an annotated data-flow diagram (ADFD) the inspectable contract between intent and implementation. In the greenfield workflow, Build, a user turns natural-language requirements into a typed graph, reviews process specifications and pre/post-conditions, ratifies generated modules, and proceeds in dependency order for Python or .NET (C#). In the brownfield workflow, Migrate uses source inference to recover an ADFD from a Fortran repository, performs target generation in bounded dependency groups, and exposes source-target alignment, generated code, errors, time, token use, and cost. The tool keeps code and artifacts on the user's machine and supports cloud or locally hosted models. Two scientific synthesis case studies produced executable systems where matched low/no-code baselines failed or were substantially less accurate. On 50 open-source Fortran repositories, the migration workflow made all 382 fixed source-oracle probes runnable and passed 327 (85.6%); two direct translation baselines each passed 83 (21.7% of planned probes). Pre-built installers and usage instructions are freely available. Tool and usage guide: https://shraddhasurana.github.io/dhaani/. Video: https://youtu.be/SShWwOMgJ9c.
comment: 4 pages, 4 figures
☆ Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
Tobias Philipp
AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.

☆ When to Test, Repair, or Regenerate: Decision-Guided Efficient RTL Generation
Feiyang Pan, Shenghe Zheng, Pengfei Xiao, Chunyan Yin, Guangbin Dou
Large language models (LLMs) can generate register-transfer-level (RTL) designs from natural-language specifications. To improve functional correctness, many RTL agents use simulation feedback to guide refinement. However, without a reference testbench, generating one for every initial implementation incurs inference cost even when the RTL is correct. We therefore introduce an adaptive harness that uses a specialized decision model to orchestrate testing, refinement, and candidate selection. It accepts high-scoring initial implementations and generates testbenches for the rest. When further search is needed, the initial score guides repair--regeneration allocation, while defect rankings and simulation feedback guide repair. For final selection, the harness prioritizes test-passing candidates and ranks them using decision-model scores. Across three benchmarks, the harness with DeepSeek improves mean Pass@1 by 5.4--7.1 percentage points over initial implementations and reduces aggregate estimated inference cost by 11.0--14.3% relative to a testbench-guided repair baseline with the same candidate cap.
☆ The Defect Is in the Arithmetic Between the Files: Static Detection of Exactly-Once Violations in Payment Pipelines
Abhishek Sharma
Whether a streaming payment pipeline charges a customer twice after a restart turns on a comparison nobody performs: how long the provider remembers an idempotency key, against how stale a record can be when the pipeline processes it for the second time. The first number is in the provider's documentation. The second is not written anywhere. It is assembled from a checkpoint interval in one file, a recovery assumption in a runbook, a restart delay in a third and a source's lateness bound in a fourth. Each file is defensible alone; the fault is in the relation between them. We give a checker that gathers those facts and states the relations, and a synthesiser that turns 335 of the 515 findings into a runnable scenario: these records, kill the job here, bring it back after this long, and this is the observable. 245 of them produce two charges. The central measurement is how far apart the evidence lies. Across a corpus of 630 pipelines we generated, 210 of them cannot be derived from fewer than three artifacts, and no single artifact yields more than 35 of the 305 duration findings. Executing the witnesses corrected our own rules: two were demoted after their scenarios produced a repeated call the provider's idempotency absorbed rather than a second charge. All 16 selected live witnesses reproduced their predicted observable against a real Kafka broker with a real process kill, and a matched control in which the provider never forgets the key did not, attributing the second charge to the key lifetime, not the replay. Fault injection finds the same defects only if the tester already assumed a long enough outage: one willing to simulate five minutes finds 15% of them, and 12 hours is needed for all. A sweep also locates a configuration with no application-level fix, where above a 14-minute recovery assumption the transaction timeout required to survive it exceeds the broker's own cap.

☆ VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
Saeid Rajabi, Chengmo Yang, Satwik Patnaik
Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

☆ Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
Leizhen Zhang, Sheng Chen
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.

☆ Automated Safety Analysis for Agentic Workflows ICSE 2027
Yanju Chen, Ying Li, Bosi Zhang, Hanzhi Liu, Hongbo Wen, Yufei Ding, Yuan Tian, Yu Feng
LLM applications are increasingly built as agentic workflows: programs that combine model calls, external tools, and control logic to act autonomously on a user's behalf. Because these workflows execute real-world actions, logical flaws in how a workflow is wired can cause severe harm in deployed systems. Unlike prompt injections or malformed API calls, these workflow bugs stem from defects in the workflow's design, yet no existing tool can statically validate workflow logic across frameworks prior to deployment. We present Apsis, a static safety analyzer that detects workflow bugs before deployment. To operate across frameworks, Apsis lifts framework-specific code into a common intermediate representation (IR). This IR models a workflow as a semantic graph of steps, data dependencies, and shared state, while annotating each component with behavioral properties such as whether an input is mandatory or how a shared channel merges concurrent writes. Building on this representation, we introduce a bug description language that formalizes recurring classes of agentic failures as declarative patterns over the IR. By matching these patterns against the IR, Apsis detects structural and behavioral flaws and pinpoints the exact step responsible for each bug. To evaluate Apsis, we construct, to our knowledge, the first corpus of workflow bugs, distilled from real-world reports across 13 widely used frameworks. On a reproducible benchmark suite drawn from this corpus, Apsis detects workflow bugs with 91% precision and 84% recall, and uncovers 36 previously unknown bugs in real-world workflows.

☆ Human-in-the-Loop Runbook Improvement with Agentic Support Automation
Rocker D'Antonio, Harry Xie
Operational support is an important component of production software services. Support requests are often emergent and can come in many forms such as customer escalations or unplanned service interruption. Engineers across organizations have been successful in implementing automation to help streamline support processes but many solutions remain in the hands of human operators. A successful strategy to improve operator response times is to maintain up-to-date runbooks which are documents enumerating triage steps and remediation procedures in the face of identified incidents. This paper is an investigation into an operational system which incorporates Agentic AI into a runbook based incident resolution pattern. The bot uses information in the runbook corpus along with some system-specific tooling to guide the manual operator through the mitigation process then evaluate the outcome and suggest edits to the runbook where it found gaps and in its ability to triage the situation. By using the runbook as a medium to bridge humans and automation, the process maintains explainability and can be decoupled from the agent system. This paper demonstrates a collaboration between human operators and Agentic AI with results from an 17 week study involving 232 production incidents. We conclude with lessons on integrating LLMs into DevOps workflows, related work in AI-assisted operations, and guidance for reproducibility.

♻ ☆ SWE-Pruner Pro: The Coder LLM Already Knows What to Prune EACL 2027

Pruning long context for coding agents has been a vital technology for efficient context management. Based on this finding, we propose SWE-Pruner Pro, which prunes tool outputs directly inside the agent. Concretely, a small head turns the agent's own internal representations into a keep-or-prune label for each line, with a length-aware embedding keyed to each tool output's line count. Notably, on MiMo-V2-Flash SWE-Pruner Pro additionally raises the SWE-Bench Verified resolve rate by +3.8% and the long-context Oolong accuracy by +2.2 points.

Coding agents face new challenges in game development, where they must produce code that is not only syntactically correct but also consistent with engine-managed lifecycle, state, and networking behavior. Each task requires an agent to implement missing behavior within an established gameplay architecture. The tests evaluate Unreal's game loop, actor lifecycle, subsystems, and replication stack while directly inspecting runtime state. In 53 tasks, 119 tests additionally inspect a distinct client world to determine whether the authoritative server state is correctly replicated. To our knowledge, this is the first coding benchmark to evaluate cross-client replication. Across 11 model-harness configurations, the best-scoring configuration achieves 46.4% pass@1, while 43 tasks remain unsolved by every evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate that compilation and shallow verification overestimate agents' ability to implement behavior that remains correct during full engine execution.

SaltBench asks how a machine referee changes how a coding agent works. Outcomes are decided outside the agent's toolchain; on the Claude lane a wall probed before any scored run isolates the agent from the network, reference solutions and harness, and 5 Gemini-lane cells served web search results are declared and leave every comparison; a dated freeze of predictions authorizes each run; a budget stop is a halt, never a failure. Five Rust systems components on a pinned Verus toolchain are each refereed by a withheld test suite. The arms: plain; salt-diet, also instructed to specify and verify its code (a registered reduced rendering of the method); and two arms handed the specification a priori, where the registered sign test at k=4 reached no verdict (3 of 4, p = 0.3125). salt-diet cost more on all five components, by a practical margin: no premium exceeded 2.8879x under either reading of the declared set and the three cheapest sat below 1.4x, a bound of this population and not a promise about larger ones: the premium is near 1 on the smallest components and rises with size. Versions 2 and 3 add the complete pilot matrix: 200 conditions over four models, 181 with a result of record, 16 inexpressible and 3 declared unreached at the cost cap, with no verdict on the arms. Version 3 adds a correctness reading, declared post hoc and registered after every verdict it reads existed and many had been read by its author: 447 cells pass the withheld suite, 40 fail, 10 are censored at a registered budget, 4 are unscorable and 42 are read by condition. salt-diet's pass-rate interval lies wholly below plain's on 8 greenfield and 5 brownfield rows and wholly above it on 2 greenfield rows. It is descriptive, over three cells of record per condition, with no test, and says nothing about whether the method makes code more or less correct. The full record is public.

♻ ☆ Formally-Verifiable and Human-Interpretable RTL Generation with LLM-Guided Stepwise Refinement
You Li, Samuel Mandell, David Z. Pan
Large language models (LLMs) are accelerating register-transfer level (RTL) development, but ensuring the correctness of generated designs remains a major challenge. Existing LLM-driven workflows rely heavily on simulation-based verification, which provides limited correctness guarantees, and often offer little insight into the design decisions behind the generated RTL. We present a framework for LLM-guided, correct-by-construction RTL generation that combines the generative capabilities of LLMs with the mathematical rigor of stepwise refinement. The framework translates natural-language requirements into a formal hardware contract and progressively refines the contract into an implementation. At each refinement step, the LLM proposes a design decision, while the refinement engine applies the corresponding transformation only after formally verifying its correctness. The resulting program is formally verified against the contract and then translated into synthesizable RTL. The recorded derivation allows every line of generated RTL to be traced back to the design decisions and requirements that motivated it. Beyond generating verified implementations, the framework provides reliable verification feedback and reusable design experience, laying the foundation for self-improving hardware generation.
♻ ☆ When the Next Step Is Not One Step: Distribution-Aware Execution Modeling for Concurrent Go Programs

Predicting the next scheduler event of a concurrent program is ill-posed as single-label classification: repeated runs from the same trace prefix produce different, equally valid next events. We formulate next-event prediction for concurrent Go programs as estimating an empirical next-event distribution obtained from repeated executions, and release a benchmark with 945 training examples from hand-written and generated programs and 798 held-out predictions on 54 real-world GoKer bug kernels from systems such as CockroachDB, Kubernetes, gRPC and etcd. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with low-rank adapters under a cross-entropy objective and a KL-to-empirical-distribution objective and compare them with zero-shot models and trivial baselines. The outcome is a neutral-to-negative result. The fine-tuned adapters (re-evaluated: 36.3% cross-entropy, 33.6% KL; originally reported 36.2% and 35.8%) are statistically indistinguishable from always predicting the majority event (35.5%), and an event n-gram model reaches 33-34%. Because each held-out prompt carries labels from about five runs, no deterministic predictor can exceed 58.9% top-1 accuracy, so we report macro-F1, balanced accuracy, per-class recall, program-clustered confidence intervals and binned calibration measured directly on both adapters. A sensitivity study with 100 runs per program shows that five-run targets are noisy (mean total-variation distance 0.24 from a 100-run reference), which plausibly limits what the KL objective can learn. This split, however, is defined in pixels, so the spatial frequencies each band covers, as seen by the viewer, change with the display and the viewing distance. Making the model explicit and expressing it in cycles per degree gives a version of SSIM that takes the viewing conditions into account while preserving its simplicity. The resulting metric, MB-SSIM, keeps SSIM's per-patch product of similarity ratios; the bands are placed where psychophysics places the visual system's channels, and the viewing geometry enters through a single number, the angular sampling density in pixels per degree. On the CID:IQ dataset, which rates the same 690 images at two viewing distances, one set of sub-band weights fitted jointly and evaluated on held-out content reaches a pooled PLCC of 0.834 against 0.787 for SSIM and 0.808 for MS-SSIM; on LIVE Release 2, calibrating the geometry yields 0.956 against 0.946 and 0.950. As a cross-verification, the CID:IQ weights applied unchanged to the Brightcove-Kingston multi-screen video dataset, which rates the same clips on a television, a tablet and a phone, give a pooled PLCC of 0.844 across devices where SSIM and MS-SSIM, which must return one number per clip, fall to 0.62 and 0.59. Accuracy is flat from three channels to six and insensitive to filter shape, window and peak placement; only the channel bandwidths matter, and the psychophysically measured values are a safe choice. The most sensitive parameter is SSIM's own stabilising constant: reducing it to a third raises the pooled PLCC to 0.857. Source code reproducing the results is available.

We argue that these criteria, while essential, are insufficient for understanding how LLMs may affect postpartum care. LLMs enter an information ecology in which women are already required to reconcile competing forms of expertise, determine whether their experiences are normal or concerning, and decide when and where to seek care. At the same time, online representations of motherhood and femininity shape which postpartum experiences are made visible and what forms of self-management are expected of women. Drawing together research on postpartum care gaps, online help-seeking, influencer cultures, gendered responsibility, and AI-supported health information, we position LLMs as emerging intermediaries within this broader care infrastructure. Because the verifier accepts the human-reference answer, advanced solver capabilities and resulting improved recovery of the physical ground truth may instead strengthen the human-machine separation. A multidimensional human usability study yields corresponding human acceptance rates of 78%, 90%, and 76%, while maintaining competitive efficiency and satisfaction. Further analysis demonstrates that advanced LALMs tend toward physical ground truth. These results show that reverse-capability verification substantially reduces machine acceptance while retaining high human acceptance through an approach different from conventional CAPTCHAs.

Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted suffix remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk generation. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and generation time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.

This study empirically tests the applicability of Fitts' List within physical Human-Robot Collaboration, by conducting a user study (N=26, within-subject design) to evaluate four distinct allocations of position/force control between human and robot in an abstract blending task. We hypothesize that the function in which humans control the position achieves better performance and receives higher user ratings. When allocating position control to the human and force control to the robot, compared to the opposite case, we observed a significant improvement in preventing overblending. This was also perceived better in terms of physical demand and overall system acceptance, while participants experienced greater autonomy, more engagement and less frustration. An interesting insight was that the supervisory role (when the robot controls both position and force) was rated second best in terms of subjective acceptance. Another surprising insight was that if position control was delegated to the robot, the participants perceived much lower autonomy than when the force control was delegated to the robot. These findings empirically support applying Fitts' principles to static function allocation for physical collaboration, while also revealing important nuanced user experience trade-offs, particularly regarding perceived autonomy when delegating position control.

The findings demonstrate trade-offs between evidential constraints, decision consistency and abstention, rather than overall superiority of the integrated framework. The mechanism is what we call silent ingestion: the agent accepts faulted data as valid on first contact without retrying or flagging the problem, then builds a fabricated answer on top of it. We show that fabrication is reducible: a verification-first Monitor, grounding checks in structured tool outputs and issuing corrective directives rather than hard blocks, raises correct recovery from 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication from 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication (+8.3pp), so deliberation guards against silent ingestion. We release RetryRealistic, the fault-injection toolkit, and all annotated traces at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/RetryRealistic

Under it, 22 aftermarket devices become components, Periphery falls to 25 and 25 products sit outside both regimes. Seven retrospective walkthroughs suggest that, for third-party products, vulnerability information stops in the vehicle manufacturer's own inventory, triggers or exploitation assessment, and that no provision obliges a product maker to tell a vehicle manufacturer: the only defined two-way route is a contract. For broader action coverage, the Candidate Actions Builder supplements AXTree-derived and system actions with VLM-provided text bindings for task-specific text entry and coordinates for widget-free interactions. ScopeAct requires only 5.3 and 4.6 VLM calls per task under the extended and official evaluation settings, respectively. In the digital era, these traces increasingly emerge through social media footprints and web search behavior at a global scale. Information seeking is globally dominated by politics and health, while regional distributions show varying degrees of divergence. Crisis periods are associated with both shared and regionally differentiated shifts. Entertainment and sports attention likewise combine globally prominent interests with regional differentiation. Overall, our findings suggest that web search data provide a valuable computational lens for observing collective attention at scale, acting as a living archive of how societal priorities vary across countries and change over time.

Several government-school teachers did not use AI to mark quizzes even though the quizzes had answer keys, because they expected students to look for evidence of the teacher's effort. Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to protect sensitive data in visualization, but understanding how privacy-induced noise affects visual representations remains fragmented. Prior work has examined the impact of DP noise on specific chart types, yet these findings are typically tied to particular chart types and evaluation settings, making it difficult to generalize across contexts. In parallel, visualization research has long established that visual channels, the visual properties of marks that encode data attributes, differ in perceptual effectiveness under noise-free conditions. However, these principles have not been systematically revisited under DP, where noise is deliberately introduced into the data to protect privacy. In this paper, we present a channel-centric perspective to reframe prior empirical and theoretical results. Our synthesis drawson prior findings to motivate a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis: the utility of DP visualizations may depend on the task-relevant reads made salient by visual channel configurations and DP mechanism choice jointly. Moreover, this perspective highlights the role of channel choice throughout the privacy-preserving visualization pipeline, from disclosure framing and DP algorithm design to utility evaluation and interpretation of noisy outputs. The synthesis also identifies gaps in the existing evaluation literature and highlights research opportunities for channel-aware DP visualization.

Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. First, structural equation modeling identified strong associations among perceived consistency across displays, presence, and self-reported restorative responses, consistent with our theoretically motivated model. Second, exploratory comparisons across video-presentation configurations revealed modest differences in consistency and restoration ratings, although these AI-generated videos did not significantly outperform the advertisement reference. Third, qualitative analysis of open-ended responses identified fascination, immersion, and restorative feelings, alongside concerns about naturalness, visual quality, and motion-related discomfort. Together, these findings provide empirical insights into MDS-mediated nature experiences, with implications for nature-video design and questionnaire refinement. They also inform a tentative conceptual extension of the model incorporating additional perceptual and evaluative factors.
☆ Crisis Governance at the Joints. Mapping the Ethical and Societal Territory of Crisis Management Technologies: The Case of Human-Swarm Teaming
Anthony Longo
Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.
comment: 3 figures
☆ Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
Rohith Pasula, Johari Dramiga, Viraj Shah, Suzan Halim, Tyler Dooskin
Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.
☆ Open Response Explorer: a Structured Collaborative Writing System for Peer-Informed Open-Response Assignments
Ziwei Gu, Ruixuan Chen, Elena Glassman
Peer-informed open-response assignments (where students view, connect, and learn from peer contributions) hold the potential to foster collaborative knowledge building, yet the unstructured nature of free-form prose prevents students from effectively comparing and making sense of peers' work. We present Open Response Explorer, an interface that recenters open responses on structured idea units through purpose-based writing and peer response exploration, augmented by common-role text segment highlighting for easy comparison. A within-subjects lab study (N=12) validated the usefulness and usability of the system, demonstrating how it shaped the open-response drafting and peer exploration practices. We discuss implications for purpose-centered authoring and exploration that transform free-form prose into structured, comparable, and collectively navigable knowledge artifacts.
☆ CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
Shwetanshu Singh, Mark Keavney, Mathieu Duteil, Meriem Mehri, Scott Blain
Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures
☆ A Human-Centric Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Digital Twin Framework for Cyber-Physical Systems
Clarisa Grijalva-Lugo, Yu-Zheng Lin, Shalaka Satam, Sicong Shao, Jesus Pacheco, Soheil Salehi, Pratik Satam
Digital twins of cyber-physical systems must operate with scarce data, on assets that change after deployment, and for humans whose needs differ, yet existing implementations fix fidelity at design time and do not match the representation to the human or the task. This paper proposes a human-centric adaptive multi-fidelity digital twin framework that models the evolving human, the physical twin, and the digital twin core, and adds a human inference and adaptation function that estimates the human state, predicts the response, and adapts the representation. The framework defines low-, medium-, and high-fidelity tiers distinguished by adaptivity and by coupling, quantified as the ratio of the digital twin latency to the duration of the process step it follows. Three proof-of-concept instantiations are evaluated: a virtual reality tutor, a computer numerical control milling model, and an industrial training station. The low tier estimated learner sentiment with an accuracy of 0.86. The forecasters of the milling model and the training station, both medium-tier, showed a normalized error decline of 0.39 to 0.89 and a human adaptation gain of 1.16 to 1.51, but their latency exceeded the physical process step by 25 to 87 times. Only the station's vision model met the physical step. The tiers are separated by which functions adapt and where the latency constraint lies, not by a monotone increase in gain or coupling.

♻ ☆ AI-Assisted Hypothesis Generation for Hospital Quality Improvement
Patrick Vossler, Jean Feng, Venkat Sivaraman, Robert Gallo, Hemal Kanzaria, Dana Freiser, Christopher Ross, Amy Ou, James Marks, Susan Ehrlich, Christopher Peabody, Lucas Zier
Hospital quality improvement (QI) programs generally proceed in two stages: (1) hypothesis generation, which identifies candidate factors that may improve care quality and efficiency, and (2) confirmatory analyses, which implement and evaluate QI initiatives targeting these factors. Although most research focuses on the confirmatory stage, hypothesis generation is equally important because it shapes where teams focus their effort. Currently, hypothesis generation depends on expert-driven, qualitative methods (e.g., Lean Healthcare tools) that can be anecdotal, hard to reproduce, time-consuming, and resource-intensive. Large language models (LLMs) could accelerate this process by analyzing clinical notes at scale, but existing AI tools can only scale up well-defined tasks, whereas hypothesis generation is a "fuzzy," exploratory, and iterative process. We propose treating not only LLM instructions but also the problem specification and validation process as tunable natural-language (hyper)parameters. Through a procedure we term "Human-AI Spec-Solution Co-Optimization," we iteratively elicit clinical experts' definitions and judgments while aligning the AI pipeline with their intended criteria. We retrospectively applied this framework at an urban safety-net hospital to length of stay and 30-day unplanned readmissions. The final pipelines screen patient charts for potential factors and filter for clinically relevant ones by self-rating, and these self-ratings achieved over 70% concordance with human experts (within one Likert point) on held-out encounters. When scaled up hospital-wide, the pipelines identified a superset of the candidate factors found in prior, primarily manual analyses. By providing auditable reasoning traces and quantifying factor prevalence, the pipelines support a more quantitative and reproducible way to prioritize factors for prospective QI interventions.
♻ ☆ A Quasi-experimental Study of Conversational AI-supported Engagement in Large CS Courses
Neha Rani, Sharan Majumder, Ishan Bhardwaj, Pedro Guillermo Feijoo Garcia
Lucrative career prospects and creative opportunities often attract students to enroll in computer science courses, resulting in large class sizes. A common challenge in large classrooms is the lack of engagement between students and both the instructor and the learning material. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) present an opportunity to leverage Conversational Artificial Intelligence (CAI) to address this challenge. To examine the potential of CAI to support engagement with learning material, we designed an in class activity in a large Software Engineering course in which students interacted with a CAI tool. Using a quasi-experimental, within-subject study design in a real classroom at a large public United States University. We compared student engagement during an activity that involved the use of CAI for discussion with an activity that did not (peer discussion). For our analysis, we collected data on students interactions with the CAI tool and their self-reported responses on multiple engagement scales. Results show higher student engagement with the learning material in the activity involving CAI discussion as opposed to without (peer discussion). Higher self-reported learning was also observed in the activity with CAI as compared to without. Students also reported significantly more usefulness for learning in the CAI condition. Overall, our results indicate that CAI (ChatGPT) has the potential to support engagement with learning content during in-class activities in large class sizes.
♻ ☆ Does AI Assistance Preserve or Collapse Disagreement? A Study of Pre-Annotations in Ambiguous Video Labeling ICML 2026
Juan Gutiérrez, Victor Gutiérrez-García, José Luis Blanco-Murillo
AI-generated Pre-Annotations can accelerate video labeling, but they may also anchor annotators to model priors and suppress disagreement that is valuable for pluralistic dataset construction. We study this tradeoff in ambiguous temporal video annotation, where annotators choose event boundaries and assign context-dependent labels such as "normal" or "abnormal." We introduce a controlled audit protocol that separates annotation cost, consensus alignment, inter-annotator consistency, temporal-boundary variation, semantic-label variation, latent-space standardization, and edit behavior. In a counterbalanced pilot study with 18 annotators and 180 annotation sessions, a fixed CLIP-based Pre-Annotation engine reduced mean annotation time by 23.11%; 72% of annotators were faster with assistance, with a median per-annotator gain of 35%. Assistance increased inter-annotator consistency and CLIP-space standardization, while semantic-label entropy changed only slightly in aggregate. A six-annotator human consensus diagnostic showed comparable alignment across conditions (AMI $\approx 0.64$ in both conditions), but this diagnostic is self-including and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as independent evidence that model influence is absent. Overall, the results suggest that Pre-Annotations acted mainly as editable temporal scaffolds in this pilot setting, while leaving open the possibility of subtler semantic anchoring effects. We contribute an audit framework and anonymized interaction traces for studying when AI-assisted annotation preserves, reshapes, or collapses human disagreement.
